 You may be able to get a private student loan without completing the FAFSA, but skipping the form could mean missing out on federal loans and other financial aid.
 Amy DeYoung Special to USA TODAY Nov. 18, 2026, 5:26 p.m. ET Hear this story Private student loans are available without completing the Free Application for Federal Student Aid (FAFSA).
 Even if you believe your income is too high, it is still recommended to complete the FAFSA to understand all your financial aid options.
 Private lenders base loan eligibility on factors like credit history and income, not the FAFSA.
 If you can't file a Free Application for Federal Student Aid (FAFSA) or have decided not to apply, student loans are still available. While the FAFSA is required to qualify for federal student loans and many other types of financial aid, most private student lenders don't require it.
 Here's what to consider before skipping the FAFSA, when a private student loan might make sense and how to apply.

 You can get a private student loan without FAFSA , but skipping it could mean missing out on grants, scholarships, work-study opportunities and federal student loans, which offer benefits that private loans generally don't.
 USA TODAY Shopping: Shop sales in tech, home, fashion, beauty & more curated by our editors. Federal student loans require you to submit the FAFSA. The FAFSA is also used to determine eligibility for many state and institutional aid programs. In some cases, completing a FAFSA automatically applies for aid from your state and even the school listed on the form. However, this isn’t always the case, so visit your school's and state’s financial aid website for more information.
 You don’t have to accept federal student loans offered through FAFSA, but completing the FAFSA helps you understand your options.
 Why you should complete the FAFSA before getting a private student loan
 Completing the FAFSA can help you understand your financial aid options before deciding how much to borrow from a private lender. It's free to apply, and you may qualify for financial assistance even if you don't think your income makes you eligible.
 “Students give up consideration for many types of loans and student aid, including access to federal, state and college grants, along with federal loans and work-study programs,” explains Steven Schuetz, vice president of enrollment management at Lebanon Valley College .
 Federal student loans also offer benefits worth considering alongside private loans. Most don't require a credit check or co-signer, and they come with fixed interest rates and access to federal repayment and forgiveness programs. Depending on your credit profile, federal loans may also offer lower interest rates than private lenders.
 “There is no strict income cutoff for qualifying for aid, and not all financial aid programs are based solely on income. Completing the FAFSA is free, and college financial aid offices are happy to help students complete the form,” Schuetz adds.
 More: Are higher federal student loan rates driving more to private loans? What to do if you can't complete the FAFSA
 If you're having trouble completing the FAFSA, you may still have options for accessing federal student aid. The best next step depends on what's preventing you from submitting the form.
 “Get in contact with your high school guidance counselor or the college's financial aid office to explain your circumstances. They will help you understand your options based on your individual circumstances and assist you through the process,” advises Schuetz.
 Here are some common situations and how to address them:
 You're experiencing technical issues. If you're receiving error messages or having trouble submitting the form, use the Department of Education's FAFSA troubleshooting resources to identify and resolve the problem.
 Your parents refuse to provide financial information. You may still qualify for a Direct Unsubsidized Loan. Submit the FAFSA and indicate that your parents are unwilling to provide their information. Your school's financial aid office will determine your eligibility.
 You have unusual family circumstances. If you're unable to obtain parental information because of abuse, abandonment, estrangement, parental incarceration or other qualifying circumstances, you may be able to submit the FAFSA without it . Your school's financial aid office will review your circumstances and determine whether you qualify for a dependency override.
 If you're unable to resolve the issue before your tuition deadline, contact your school's financial aid office about available options, including payment plans or other financial assistance.
 Do private student loans require FAFSA?
 Private student loans aren’t federal loans, so you don’t need to complete the FAFSA before applying. Instead, private lenders evaluate your eligibility based on factors such as your credit history, income, debt-to-income ratio, school eligibility and enrollment status.
 Many students, particularly undergraduates with a less established credit history, may need a co-signer to qualify for a private student loan. Applying with a creditworthy co-signer can improve your chances of approval and help you secure a lower interest rate or more favorable loan terms.
 Check student loan options with College Ave When might you consider a private student loan without FAFSA?
 Although completing the FAFSA can help you explore your financial aid options, there are circumstances where applying directly for a private student loan may make sense.
 Schuetz identifies the potential for more competitive private loan rates as one reason students might choose not to complete the FAFSA. If you have strong credit or a creditworthy co-signer, you may qualify for a lower interest rate from a private lender than you'd receive on a federal student loan.
 Some additional examples include:
 You prefer not to disclose family financial information. Some students may be uncomfortable sharing their family's financial details through the FAFSA, particularly if they don't expect to qualify for need-based aid.
 Your educational program isn't eligible for federal aid. Some trade schools , apprenticeships, certificate programs and other nontraditional educational programs don't qualify for federal student aid. However, certain private lenders may finance these programs.
 You've missed a financial aid deadline or experienced delays. If you're approaching a tuition payment deadline, a private student loan may provide another financing option while you resolve FAFSA-related issues.
 Before applying, compare private loan eligibility requirements, interest rates and repayment terms. You can also check with your school's financial aid office to determine whether you're still eligible for federal or institutional assistance.
 Explore career training loans with Sallie Mae More: How to pay for trade school: Grants, FAFSA, loans and more How much can you borrow without FAFSA?
 Without FAFSA, you may be able to borrow up to your school's full cost of attendance with a private student loan, minus any other financial aid you receive. However, your borrowing limit also depends on the lender's requirements, your creditworthiness and your school's certification.
 To determine how much you need to borrow, calculate your remaining funding gap:
 Cost of attendance − scholarships and grants − savings and family contributions − other financial aid = funding gap 
 For example, if your first year of college costs $20,000, receive $10,000 in scholarships and grants and have $5,000 in savings or family contributions, you'll need another $5,000 to cover your expenses.
 You could apply for a $5,000 private student loan to cover that gap, provided you meet the lender's eligibility requirements.
 More: Financial aid isn’t enough? 6 ways to pay for the rest of college How to get a private student loan without FAFSA
 Getting a private student loan without FAFSA is similar to applying for other types of loans. Start by calculating how much you need to borrow, subtracting any scholarships, grants, savings or family contributions from your total education costs.
 Once you know how much financing you need, follow these steps:
 Research private student loan lenders. Compare lenders' eligibility requirements, advertised interest rates and repayment options. Make sure they work with your school and educational program.
 Prequalify with multiple lenders. Many lenders let you check personalized rates and estimated loan terms with a soft credit inquiry, which won't affect your credit score.
 Consider applying with a co-signer. A creditworthy co-signer may improve your chances of approval and help you qualify for a lower interest rate.
 Compare your loan options. Look at fixed versus variable interest rates, repayment terms, monthly payments and whether you'll need to make payments while you're in school.
 Submit your application. Choose a lender and complete the formal application, providing any required documentation, such as proof of identity, income and enrollment. The lender may conduct a hard credit inquiry.
 Complete the school certification process. If approved, your lender will typically contact your school to verify your enrollment and eligible borrowing amount. This process usually doesn't require much involvement from you.
 Review and accept your final loan terms. Carefully review the interest rate, repayment schedule and total borrowing costs before signing your loan agreement.
 Receive your loan funds. The lender typically disburses the money directly to your school to cover tuition and other charges. Any remaining funds are generally refunded to you for eligible education expenses.
 Explore student loan rates with Earnest How to compare private student loans without FAFSA
 When comparing private student loans, start by prequalifying with multiple lenders to see your estimated interest rates and repayment terms. Many lenders offer prequalification with a soft credit inquiry, which won't affect your credit score. Check whether a lender offers this option before submitting your information.
 Prequalification can help you compare personalized loan options rather than relying on advertised rates, which may not reflect what you'll qualify for. Keep in mind that your final rates and terms may change after you submit a formal application.
 Once you have multiple options, consider the following factors:
 Total loan cost: Compare the total amount you'll repay, including principal, interest and fees. Sallie Mae's student loan calculator can help you estimate monthly payments and overall borrowing costs.
 Fixed or variable interest rates: Fixed rates remain the same throughout the loan term, while variable rates can rise or fall over time, affecting your monthly payments and total interest costs.
 Repayment terms: Compare the available loan terms and in-school repayment options, such as immediate, interest-only or deferred payments. Making payments while you're in school can reduce your overall borrowing costs.
 Grace period: Check whether the lender offers a period after graduation or leaving school before full principal and interest payments begin. Some lenders offer six months, while others have different policies.
 Fees: Look for origination fees, late payment fees and other charges that could increase your borrowing costs. Also check whether the lender charges a prepayment penalty.
 Autopay discounts: Some lenders offer interest rate reductions for enrolling in automatic payments. Compare the discount amounts and eligibility requirements.
 Co-signer requirements and release: Determine whether you need a co-signer to qualify and whether adding one could improve your loan terms. If the lender offers co-signer release, review the requirements, including the number of on-time payments needed.
 Borrower protections and support: Compare hardship assistance, forbearance options and customer service availability. These benefits can be particularly valuable if your financial circumstances change during repayment.
 Bottom line
 You can get a private student loan without completing the FAFSA, but you could miss out on federal loans, grants and other financial aid. Even if you don't think you'll qualify for assistance, submitting the FAFSA can help you understand your options before borrowing.
 If you can't complete the FAFSA, contact your school's financial aid office to explore possible solutions. If you decide to pursue private financing, prequalify with at least three lenders and compare interest rates, total borrowing costs, repayment terms and borrower protections. Choose the student loan offer that best fits your needs and budget.
 Frequently asked questions
 Can I get a private student loan without filling out FAFSA?
 Yes, most private student loan lenders don't require you to complete the FAFSA. Instead, eligibility typically depends on your credit history, income, debt-to-income ratio and whether your school and educational program qualify for financing.
 Can I get a student loan without FAFSA or a co-signer?
 Yes, you may qualify for a private student loan without FAFSA or a co-signer if you meet the lender's credit and income requirements. However, students with limited credit histories or income may have difficulty qualifying independently. Federal student loans require the FAFSA, but most don't require a credit check or co-signer.
 What happens if I don't fill out FAFSA?
 If you don't complete the FAFSA, you generally won't qualify for federal student loans, Pell Grants or federal work-study programs. You could also miss out on state and institutional financial aid that uses FAFSA information to determine eligibility. However, you can still apply for private student loans and scholarships that don't require the FAFSA.
 Should I fill out the FAFSA if my parents make too much money?
 Yes, completing the FAFSA is worthwhile even if your parents have a high income. There's no universal income cutoff for federal student aid, and eligibility depends on more than family income alone. Even if you don't qualify for need-based grants, you may still be eligible for federal Direct Unsubsidized Loans and other financial assistance.
 Do you need FAFSA for Sallie Mae or other private student loans?
 No, Sallie Mae and most other private student loan lenders don't require the FAFSA. Instead, lenders evaluate factors such as your creditworthiness, income and school eligibility. You may also need a creditworthy co-signer to qualify or secure more favorable loan terms.
